prompt.context: Many non-OECD countries suffer from frequent blackouts and shortages in electricity. This is a known fact. Following the massive earthquake in Japan in 2011, there were significant power shortages as a result of TEPCO nuclear reactors going offline. Japan was left with a deficit of nearly 2 gigawatts and turned to rental power providers who supplied 2000 MW of temporary power within 3 months. Similarly, many rapidly developing countries utilize rental power providers to bridge gaps in their electrical infrastructures. The Uganda Electricity Transmission Company (UETCL) is suffering from severe electrical shortages due to recent droughts. Uganda produces 99% of its electricity through hydroelectric power. The 250 MW Bujagali hydroelectric plant in Uganda typically produces about 1 million MWh annually when the dam reservoir is at least 100 ft deep. Due to recent droughts, the water level has fallen to 76 ft and is expected to stay around that level for the next 6 months before returning to normal. If the reservoir falls below 50 ft, no power can be produced. Production capacity decreases proportionally when the water level is below 100 ft, reaching 0% at 50 ft.
prompt.question:
This is a multi-part case. You will be asked a series of questions. No formal framework is required — think creatively through each stage.

Prompt A: List at least 3 reasons why electricity shortages occur and may be more frequent in non-OECD countries.

Prompt B: Why is the lack of electricity such a serious problem?

Prompt C: List 5 or more data points you would require to determine which countries a rental power provider should prioritize.

Prompt D: The UETCL is suffering from severe electrical shortages due to recent droughts. Why might this be?

Prompt E: Is it possible to forecast how much power the UETCL will require during a drought? If yes or no, please explain why.

Prompt F: Calculate what the electricity shortage will be for the next 12 months (given the drought scenario described).

Prompt G: Based on your answer from Prompt F, calculate how many Ugandans will be without electricity during the next 6 months — provide both the actual number and the percentage. Assume even power distribution across the country.

clarifying_info.a: OECD countries include all wealthy European and North American countries as well as Australia and New Zealand.

clarifying_info.q: What type of power does Uganda primarily use?
clarifying_info.a: Uganda produces 99% of its electricity through hydroelectric power.

clarifying_info.q: For the drought calculation, should I assume even production throughout the year?
clarifying_info.a: Yes. Assume even power production for every month of the year, with the only varying factor being the drought. Also assume a linear function of depth vs. power producing capacity.

clarifying_info.q: What is Uganda's annual power consumption?
What percentage of Uganda's population already lacks access to electricity?
clarifying_info.a: 28% of the population has no access to electricity.

clarifying_info.q: Is the 250 MW installed capacity relevant to the calculation?
clarifying_info.a: The 250 MW figure is extraneous information for this calculation. MW are units of power; MWh are units of energy (power used over time). Work with the MWh figures provided.

framework: No formal framework required (BCG-style conversational case)
Structure thinking around: causes of shortage → economic/social impact → market prioritization criteria → technical diagnosis → forecasting approach → quantitative calculation → population impact

questions.prompt: Prompt A: Why do electricity shortages occur more frequently in non-OECD countries? List at least 3 reasons.
questions.guidance: Encourage the candidate to brainstorm broadly. Award credit for any well-reasoned answer. Strong candidates will list 5+ distinct reasons covering infrastructure, funding, demand-side growth, and external shocks.

questions.prompt: Prompt B: Why is the lack of electricity such a serious problem?
questions.guidance: Push candidates beyond 'no TV, no light.' Strong answers address: lower productivity; poorer education, healthcare, quality of life; limited access to information; and political instability. Best candidates note that electricity access has become a de facto right, and that blackouts restricting information access can spur revolts. Also relevant: Africa's leapfrog to mobile phones created massive new electrical demand. The rental power provider industry has been doubling every 3-4 years as a result.

questions.prompt: Prompt C: List 5 or more data points needed to determine which countries a rental power provider should prioritize.
questions.guidance: Basic data points: population, population growth, per capita GDP, GDP, GDP growth. Intermediate: fossil fuel production, energy generation/consumption, power outages per year. Advanced: % of electrical production from hydroelectric power (high hydro reliance = drought vulnerability), electrical grid utilization rates (high utilization = greater blackout risk during peak load), political and financial risk rankings, corruption levels. Strong candidates reach the advanced tier unprompted.

questions.prompt: Prompt D: The UETCL is suffering from severe shortages due to recent droughts. Why might this be?
questions.guidance: Candidates are not expected to know this without guidance. If struggling, hint that Uganda produces 99% of electricity via hydroelectric power. The correct reasoning: in drought conditions, water levels fall, rivers flow more slowly, and the amount of electricity that can be generated drops significantly.

questions.prompt: Prompt E: Is it possible to forecast how much power the UETCL will require during a drought?
questions.guidance: Yes. Forecast energy production by examining water levels, power plant efficiency, and historical production data. The reservoir water level is the most variable factor and can be estimated using rainfall forecasts and knowledge of the hydroelectric grid. Power consumption tracks GDP growth — when GDP grows, consumption grows proportionally. Therefore: production forecast = rainfall + hydro grid model; consumption forecast = GDP/economic forecasts. Both are typically publicly available.

questions.prompt: Prompt F: Calculate the electricity shortage for the next 12 months given: normal production = 1,000,000 MWh/year; reservoir currently at 76 ft (drought for 6 months); 100 ft = full production; 50 ft = 0 production; linear relationship.
questions.guidance: The 250 MW installed capacity is extraneous. Use the linear depth-to-capacity relationship. Two equivalent solution paths are acceptable.

math.setup: Linear scale: 50 ft = 0%, 100 ft = 100%. Each foot above 50 ft = 2% capacity. At 76 ft: (76 - 50) x 2% = 52% production capacity. Normal 6-month production = 500,000 MWh. Drought 6-month production = 52% x 500,000 = 260,000 MWh.
steps: Alternative: 1 ft of water above 50 ft = 1,000,000/50 = 20,000 MWh/year; deficit = (100 - 76) x 20,000 = 480,000 MWh/year; for 6-month drought: 480,000 / 2 = 240,000 MWh
math.answer: 240,000 MWh shortage over the next 12 months

questions.prompt: Prompt G: Based on the 240,000 MWh shortage, how many Ugandans will be without electricity during the next 6 months? Provide the actual number and percentage.
questions.guidance: Candidate must ask for additional data before it is supplied: Uganda annual consumption = 2,000,000 MWh; population = 34,500,000; population already without electricity = 28%. Key insight: calculate per-capita consumption only for the electrified population, then divide the shortage by per-capita consumption to find newly affected people, then add those already without power.

math.setup: Population already without power = 34,500,000 x 28% = 9,660,000 (round to 10,000,000). Population with power = 34,500,000 - 10,000,000 = 24,500,000 (round to 25,000,000). Semi-annual per capita consumption = 2,000,000 MWh / 25,000,000 people / 2 = 0.04 MWh/person.
steps: Additional people losing power due to drought = 240,000 MWh / 0.04 MWh/person = 6,000,000
math.answer: 16,000,000 Ugandans (~46% of the population) will be without electricity during the next 6 months

brainstorming.prompt: List data points a rental power provider would use to prioritize which countries to enter.

categories.name: Energy supply
ideas: Age and condition of power plants

categories.name: Demand-side risk
ideas: High GDP growth outpacing infrastructure investment

recommendation: Rental power providers should prioritize rapidly developing non-OECD countries with high GDP growth, fast population growth, aging electrical infrastructure, high grid utilization rates, and significant hydroelectric dependency (which creates drought-related vulnerability)

Uganda is a strong candidate: it has a near-total reliance on hydro power, is experiencing drought-driven shortages affecting ~46% of its population, and has a clear quantifiable gap of 240,000 MWh that rental power can fill
risks: Political and financial instability in target markets may make contract enforcement and payment collection difficult
Countries with high corruption levels create operational and reputational risks
Hydro dependency may resolve if rainfall normalizes, limiting contract duration
Currency risk and repatriation of profits in frontier markets
next_steps: Conduct country-by-country scoring on the prioritization data points from Prompt C
Quantify addressable market size (shortage MWh x price per MWh) for top-ranked countries
Assess political/financial risk ratings for shortlisted markets before committing capital
Model contract structures that account for short-term drought cycles vs. structural infrastructure gaps
